# Introduction

`QC_notebook` is the first of a series of ready-to-do-DataAnalysis. The aim is to turn complex and vast data analysis workflows
into user-friendly ready-to-use tools for neuro-scientist.

The framework is based on SingleCellExperiment (SCE) project, where in a single object users can combine different single-cell experiments, i.e. expression or epigenetic data. In addition, several different types of information for both genes or cells. With additional metadata space to store, for instance, literature references.

For more information, visit [SCE](https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/SingleCellExperiment/inst/doc/intro.html).


# Libraries

```{r message=FALSE}
library(HDF5Array)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(cellhashR)
library(DropletUtils)
library(scater)
library(scuttle)
library(scales)
library(ggExtra)
```

It's important to set a seed for reproducibility. This is used by algorithms which has a randomized initiation.

```{r}
set.seed(12)
```

In case you want to check the content of your `.h5` file you can run:

```{r eval=FALSE}
# rna-seq & atac-seq
h5ls("data/muA/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
# hto tags
h5ls("data/muA/muAh/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
```



# Data Loading & SCE object creation

To load the information contained on a h5 file, use `read10xCounts` because it handles automatically the loading of both mRNA data and ATAC data. `read10xCounts` returns a SCE object with all the information. Make sure to split the data so the object contains two separated experiments, one for gene expression and the other for epigenetics, `peaks`.


```{r}
# Loading data
sce <- read10xCounts("data/muA/filtered_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
# spitting by type, i.e. mRNA & ATAC sequencing
sce <- splitAltExps(sce, rowData(sce)[, "Type"])
# remember to swap experiments to work with the count matrix of your experiment
sce <- swapAltExp(sce, "Gene Expression")

# set row names as unique to avoid redundancy
rownames(sce) <- make.unique(rowData(sce)$Symbol)
# set colnames as the cell barcode
colnames(sce) <- colData(sce)$"Barcode"
```


```{r}
sce
```


*To add HTOs as metadata, remember to perform the intersection counts-htos*

The process is repeated, load the data using `read10xCounts` function, set the column names and then perform the intersection.

```{r}
# using DropletUtils::read10xCounts
htos <- read10xCounts("data/muA/muAh/raw_feature_bc_matrix.h5")
colnames(htos) <- htos$Barcode
htos <- htos[, intersect(colnames(sce), colnames(htos))]
```

```{r}
# make sure that the colnames are the same in both assays
stopifnot(setequal(colnames(htos), colnames(sce)))
```

Lastly, add the hto data as an alternative experiment.

```{r}
altExp(sce, "hto") <- SummarizedExperiment(assay(htos))

# hto can be removed

#rm(htos)
```

# Demultiplexing

Now the objective is to demultiplex the data and obtain the HTO tag which was used for each cell.

```{r}
# make sure to have Python installed with all the required packages if you want to run 'gmm_demux'
reticulate::py_config()
```

Set a list containing the HTO tags of interest. It will be used to filter out those non interesting tags.

```{r}
HTO_tag=c("HTO-1","HTO-2","HTO-3","HTO-4","HTO-5","HTO-6","HTO-7","HTO-8","HTO-9","HTO-10")
```


```{r include=FALSE}
#' @title demultiplexer
#' @description demultiplexer calls cellhashR::GenerateCellHashingCalls. Filtering of the
#' matrix of counts is performed prior call of the function.
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment object.
#' @param methods List containing the algorithms to be used for the demultiplexing. This includes
#' "multiseq", "gmm_demux", "htodemux", "dropletutils".
#' @param project Character vector to use to name the project under the directory of pdf/1-Loading. The PDFs output from GenerateCellHashigCalls will be saved to this directory. Default to "New_project".
#' @param HTO_tag List of character strings containing the name of the HTO tags to keep, the white-list
#' @param filter_singlet Boolean parameter to specify whether the resulting assay should be filtered to keep only cell barcodes assigned as singlets. Default to FALSE.
#' @return A SingleCellExperiment object with information of consensus call and consensus call global stored in colData(sce_object).

demultiplexer <- function(sce_object,
                            methods=c("multiseq","gmm_demux", "htodemux", "dropletutils"),
                            project= "New_project",
                            HTO_tag,
                            filter_singlet=FALSE){
  require(cellhashR)
  
  if (!file.exists(file.path("pdf/1-Loading",project))){
    dir.create(file.path("pdf/1-Loading",project))
  }
  
  
  barcode_df <- as.data.frame(
    assay(swapAltExp(sce_object, "hto"))[rownames(assay(swapAltExp(sce_object, "hto"))) %in% HTO_tag,])
  # demultiplexing
  pdf(file.path("pdf/1-Loading",project,"hto.pdf"), width = 20, height = 20)
  calls <- GenerateCellHashingCalls(barcodeMatrix = barcode_df,
                                  methods = methods, 
                                  doTSNE = FALSE,
                                  majorityConsensusThreshold = 0.3)
  # create summary plots to contrast cells based on call-status. Help inform why some cells were not called
  SummarizeCellsByClassification(calls = calls, barcodeMatrix = barcode_df)
  dev.off()
  
  stopifnot(setequal(colnames(sce_object), calls$cellbarcode))
  colData(sce_object)$consensus_call <- calls$consensuscall
  colData(sce_object)$consensus_call_global <- calls$consensuscall.global
  # interest in filtering by calls$consensuscall.global
  if(filter_singlet==TRUE){
    sce_object <- sce_object[, sce_object$Barcode %in% calls[ calls$consensuscall.global=="Singlet", ]$cellbarcode]
    }
  sce_object
}
```

Call `demultiplexer` function and it will take care of all your problems.

```{r}
sce <- demultiplexer(sce, HTO_tag = HTO_tag)
```


# QC metrics computation

Using addPerCellQCMetrics we can add information regarding mitochondrial and ribosomal genes in our assay, really easily.
This information is used for checking the quality of the cells in the downstream analysis.

To know more, run ?scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics

```{r}

sce <- addPerCellQCMetrics(sce, subset=list(Mito=grep("mt-", rownames(sce),value=TRUE),
                                    Ribo=grep("(^Rpl|^Rps|Mrp)", rownames(sce), value = TRUE)))
```

It's possible to set the threshold before hand, so it can be passed later to the functions.

```{r}
mito_max=15
min_nfeatures=log10(200) #be carefull how you set the threshold for number of features. For functions where the scale is log, the threshold is interpreted directly as a logarithm. However, when the scale is not log, you will need to pass a normal value.
```



# QC metrics visualization

An image is worth a thousand words...

For that reason visualizing the QC  metrics which were added before are useful to check the quality of our cells.

```{r include=FALSE}

#' @title plot_QC_Violin
#' @description plot_QC_Violin generates a violin + scatter + box plot for the variable desired.
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment object.
#' @param y Character vector from colData information of the SingleCellExperiment object to be displayed.
#' Default to `sum`which is the total count of UMIs.
#' @param ylab Character vector to be set as the label to be displayed on the Y axis.
#' @param title Character vector to be set as the title of the plot.
#' @return A graphic display of the variable specified.

plot_QC_Violin <- function(sce_object, y="sum", ylab="nCount_RNA", title="Number of UMIs", ...){
  p <- plotColData(sce_object, y=y, ...) +
    geom_point(size=0.25, alpha=0.5, position = position_jitter(width=0.25,seed = 12345))+
    geom_boxplot(width=0.025, outlier.size = 0.5, outlier.alpha = 0.8)+
    xlab(NULL)+
    ylab(ylab)+ 
    ggtitle(title)+
    theme(axis.text.y=element_text(size = 14,hjust = 0.5), title = element_text(size = 14,hjust = 0.5))
  p
  }
```

`plot_QC_Violin()` is the function designed to visualize those QC metrics.



## Examples visualizing univariate QC metrics

```{r}
plot_QC_Violin(sce)
```

To know more about what can be plotted:

```{r}
colnames(colData(sce))
```


```{r}
plot_QC_Violin(sce_object = sce, y = "subsets_Mito_percent", ylab = "percent_mito", title = NULL)
```


## Relation between nUMIs and nGenes

```{r include=FALSE}

#' @title plot_UMIvsGene
#' @description plot_UMIvsGene displays a scatter plot of the relations between log10(UMI) on X axis and log10(genes)  on Y axis. #' a linear regression is fitted to the data and displayed.
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment object. It has to contain in the colData: "sum", "detected".
#' @param colour_by A character vector to set the colour of the data points. It has to be a column in colData(sce_object). 
#' @param size_by A character vector to set the size of the data points. It has to be a column in colData(sce_object).
#' @return A  ggplot figure.

plot_UMIvsGene <- function(sce_object, colour_by = NULL, size_by=NULL, ...){
  
  p <- plotColData(sce, x="sum", y="detected",
                           colour_by=colour_by,
                           size_by=size_by, ...) +
    scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + 
    scale_colour_gradient(aesthetics = c("colour"),low = "gray90", high = "black") +
    scale_size_area(max_size = 3)+
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", show.legend = FALSE)+
    xlab("log10(nCount_RNA)")+
    ylab("log10(nFeature_RNA)") +
    theme_classic() + 
    theme(legend.position = "left") +
    labs(colour="percent.mito") +
    guides(size=guide_legend("percent.ribo"))

  p <- ggMarginal(p, type = "densigram",bins=100, fill="grey", alpha=.3)

  p
}
```


`plot_UMIvsGene` is meant to facilitate the visualization of log-transformed UMI and detected genes. It will produce a customized scatter pot, for instance axis labels. However, as it returns a ggplot object, one can override these customization.


```{r}
plot_UMIvsGene(sce_object = sce,
               colour_by = "subsets_Mito_percent",
               size_by = "subsets_Ribo_percent")
```



To plot a scatter pot, with different information, one can call ?scater::plotColData 

## Plotting a scatter plot of Genes vs percentage mitochondial

In this case it is useful to use the function `plot_QC_scatter` as one can pass thresholds for the metrics visualized. In this case, the function adds a horizontal and/or vertical line marking the threshold(s) specified by the user.


```{r include=FALSE}
#' @title plot_QC_scatter
#' @description plot_QC_scatter produces a fully customized scatter plot for two continuous variables. Furthermore, by passing 
#' thresholds for the metrics of interest, the function will add either a vertical or horizontal line, intercepting either x-axis
#' or y-axis at the specified threshold.
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment object.
#' @param x Continuous variable to be displayed in the x-axis.
#' @param y Continuous variable to be displayed in the y-axis.
#' @param xthreshold Value at which display a vertical line, marking the specified threshold.
#' @param ythreshold Value at which display a horizontal line, marking the specified threshold.
#' @return A customized scatter plot of class ggplot.

plot_QC_scatter <- function(sce_object, x, y, xthreshold=NULL, ythreshold=NULL, ...){
  p <- plotColData(sce_object, x=x, y=y, ...)
  if (!is.null(ythreshold)){p <- p + geom_hline(aes(yintercept = ythreshold), colour = "red", linetype = 2)}
  if(!is.null(xthreshold)){p <- p + geom_vline(aes(xintercept = xthreshold), colour = "red", linetype = 2)}
  if(!is.null(c(xthreshold, ythreshold))) {
    annotations <- data.frame(
      xpos = c(-Inf,-Inf,Inf,Inf),
      ypos =  c(-Inf, Inf,-Inf,Inf),
      annotateText = c(
        as.character(table(sce_object$subsets_Mito_percent <= ythreshold & sce_object$detected <= xthreshold)[2]), #BL:6
        as.character(table(sce_object$subsets_Mito_percent >= ythreshold & sce_object$detected <= xthreshold)[2]), #TL:5
        as.character(table(sce_object$subsets_Mito_percent <= ythreshold & sce_object$detected >= xthreshold)[2]), #BR: 19547
        as.character(table(sce_object$subsets_Mito_percent >= ythreshold & sce_object$detected >= xthreshold)[2])), #TR: 442
      hjustvar = c(-1,-1,5,10),
      vjustvar = c(-5,10,-5,10)
    )
    p <- p + geom_text(data = annotations, aes(x=xpos,y=ypos,hjust=hjustvar,vjust=vjustvar,label=annotateText))
  }
  p
}

```


As seen below, when passed two thresholds, the function displays the number of cells that lied at each side of the line.

```{r}
plot_QC_scatter(sce, x="detected", y="subsets_Mito_percent",
            color_by = "consensus_call_global", xthreshold = 200, ythreshold = mito_max)
```


# Set QC status

Here we want to determine what cells has (**in this specific order**):

+ More percentage of mitochondrial genes than the threshold
+ Lower number of detected genes than the threshold
+ Lied below a linear regression shifted by - 0.09

We save this information into a single column, `qc`, which can be used for statistics, plotting and filtering.


```{r include=FALSE}

#' @title set_QC_status
#' @description set_QC_status Created a column in colData indicating whether cells passed or failed three QC criterias: maximum #' mitochondrial gene percentage, minimum features (detected RNA) and laying above a linear regression line with an offset of 
#' -0.09. For the last criteria, a linear model is fitted using as formula log10(features) ~ log10(UMIs)
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperimet object containing QC metrics computed with scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics. For more
#' information ?scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics .
#' @param mito_percent_column Character string indicating the name of the column in colData. This column is added by
#' scuttle::addPerCellQCMetrics.
#' @param mito_max Numerical value indicating the threshold for the maximum percentage of mitochondrial genes. 
#' Default to 15.
#' @param min_nfeatures Numerical value indicating the threshold for the minimum of features. Default to log10(200).
#' @return

set_QC_status <- function(sce_object=NULL,
                          mito_percent_column=NULL,
                          mito_max=15,
                          min_nfeatures=log10(200)){
  
  # Assessing what cells pass the threshold for mitochondrial gene percentage
  # retrieveCellInfo looks into colData for the column passed and retrieves a list. The second element in the list contains the numerical values.
  colData(sce_object)$qc <- gsub(
    "TRUE", "passed", gsub("FALSE", "fails_maxMito", retrieveCellInfo(sce_object, by=mito_percent_column)[[2]] <= mito_max))
  # filtering by passed cells from mito_percent criteria and assess whether those cells passe or no the min_feature criteria.
  colData(sce_object)$qc <-
    replace(x=colData(sce_object)$qc,
            list=which(sce_object$qc == "passed"),
            values=gsub(
              "TRUE", "passed", gsub("FALSE", "fails_minFeat",
                                     log10(sce_object[,sce_object$qc == "passed"]$detected)>=min_nfeatures)))
  
  # fitting linear model with the formula log10(features) ~ log10(UMI)
  lm <- lm(log10(sce_object[, sce_object$qc == "passed"]$detected) ~ log10(sce_object[, sce_object$qc == "passed"]$sum))
  
  # Assessing what cells passed the criteria of laying above a linear model with a offset of -0.09.
  colData(sce_object)$qc <-
    replace(x=colData(sce_object)$qc,
            list=which(sce_object$qc =="passed"),
            values=gsub("TRUE", "passed", gsub("FALSE", "fails_lm", log10(sce_object[, sce_object$qc == "passed"]$detected) > 
                   log10(sce_object[, sce_object$qc == "passed"]$sum) * lm$coefficients[2] + (lm$coefficients[1]-.09))))
  sce_object
}
```

`set_QC_status` functions was designed to handle all that operations for you and return the information in the column `qc`. This column can be used for different statistics. It is important to take into account that once a cell fails a criteria, it is excluded from next operations.

```{r}
sce <- set_QC_status(sce_object = sce, mito_percent_column = "subsets_Mito_percent")
```

We can check the number of cells which failed each condition being:

+ fails_maxMito: for maximum percentage for mitochondrial genes.
+ fails_minFeat: for minimum number of genes.
+ fails_lm: for linear model.

```{r}
table(sce$qc)
```


Now, the visualizations can be redone, to check the characteristics of the cells when filtering by QC criteria.

Let's imagine: 

*"I wan to see the number of genes for the wells which passed all the quality control"*

```{r}
plot_QC_Violin(sce_object = sce[, sce$qc == "passed"],
               y="detected", ylab = "nGenes", title = NULL)
```


One might be interested in having a look at a particular QC metric for a particular condition. It can be easily done by passing that particular condition as `x` parameter to our function `plot_QC_Violin()`.

For more information, run `?scater::plotColData`. Or check this [tutorial](http://bioconductor.org/books/3.16/OSCA.basic/quality-control.html#common-choices-of-qc-metrics)



```{r}
plot_QC_Violin(sce_object = sce, x="consensus_call", y = "subsets_Mito_percent",
               ylab = "percent_mito", title = NULL, 
               colour_by="consensus_call") +
  geom_boxplot(alpha=.05) +
  coord_flip() + scale_x_discrete(limits=rev)
```



# Count matrix normalization

Once the QC metrics had been check, and cell had been filtered. It is time to normalize the count matrix.

To do so, one can use simple approach, such as using the log-normalize the matrix. Or, more sophisticated method such as Variance Stabilizing transformation or Analytic Pearson Residual transformation.

In the following sections, it is shown how ot proceed for all this three methods and how to visualized using UMAP representation.

Notice that all normalized counts are included in the same SCE object, allowing to have all-in-one.


## Log-normalized counts

For a simple normalization of our count matrix, one can use `logNormCounts()` from the scuttle package.

```{r eval=FALSE}
?scuttle::logNormCounts

# filtering by cell which passed all my QC criteria.
sce <- logNormCounts(sce[, sce$qc == "passed"])
```


This functions adds  second assay named as `logcounts`


```{r}
assays(sce)
```


This assay can be used to call dimensionality reduction techniques, such as UMAP.

Since computing UMAP might take several minutes for large datasets, a good idea is to set a BiocParallel object to passed to the BPPARAM parameter in runUMAP. Just modify `workers` parameter according to your machine.

```{r eval=FALSE}
?BiocParallel::MulticoreParam
bp <- BiocParallel::MulticoreParam(workers = 12, RNGseed = 16, progressbar = TRUE)
```


```{r eval=FALSE}
sce <- runUMAP(sce[, sce$qc == "passed"], BPPARAM=bp)
```

And now, simply plot UMAP


```{r eval=FALSE}
plotUMAP(sce[, sce$qc == "passed"], point_size=.05, colour_by="Sox10") +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "grey", high = "blue") +
  coord_equal() +
  guides(colour=guide_legend(NULL, override.aes = list(size=2)))
```


![](umap_logNorm.png)


To know more about what parameters one can tune, run ?scater::plotUMAP




## Variance Stabilizing transformation, a.k.a SCTransform()

For information about this technique, visit this [vignette](https://satijalab.org/seurat/articles/sctransform_vignette.html).


```{r include=FALSE}
#' @title do_vst_transform
#' @description do_vst_transform Calls sctransform::vst on the count matrix, asking for returning the correct UMI matrix.
#' The corrected UMI matrix is then log transformed. The matrix can be obtained as it is or within a SCE object, by passing TRUE
#' to the argument `as.AltExp`.
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment objec.
#' @param as.AltExp Boolean parameter to specify whether add the log-transformed count matrix as alternative experiment to the 
#' SCE object.
#' @return When `as.AltExp` is TRUE (default), the function returns a DelayedMatrix. When `as.AltExp` is TRUE, a SCE object is returned. 

do_vst_transform <- function(sce_object, as.AltExp=TRUE){
  vst <- sctransform::vst(as(assay(sce_object),'Matrix'), return_corrected_umi = TRUE)
  vst <- DelayedArray(log1p(vst$umi_corrected)/log(2))
  if (as.AltExp) {
    altExp(sce_object, "Gene_Expression_VST") <- SummarizedExperiment(list(count_vst=vst), colData = colData(sce_object))
    sce_object
  } else {vst}
}
```


```{r}    
sce <- do_vst_transform(sce[, sce$qc=="passed"])
```


Now we have out count matrix normalized stored as alternative experiment in our SCE object. Remember to swap the experiment and we are go to go for dimensionality reduction.


```{r eval=FALSE}
sce <- swapAltExp(sce, "Gene_Expression_VST")

sce <- runUMAP(sce, BPPARAM=bp, exprs_values="count_vst")
```

We can give also colors to our plots, provided that we explicitly pass the count matrix via the argument `by_exprs_values`. This is essential if our count matrix name is not `logcounts`.

```{r eval=FALSE}
plotUMAP(sce, colour_by="Sox10", point_size=.05, by_exprs_values="count_vst") +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "grey", high = "blue") +
  coord_equal() +
  guides(colour=guide_legend(NULL, override.aes = list(size=2)))
```

![](umap_vst.png)


## Analytic Pearson Residuals Normalization

To know more about this technique, check out the [publication](https://genomebiology.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s13059-021-02451-7)

```{r eval=FALSE}
sce <- swapAltExp(sce, "Gene Expression")
```


```{r read_RDS, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE}
sce <- readRDS("sce_qc.rds")
```


```{r include=FALSE}
#' @title do_AnPearson_transform
#' @description do_AnPearson_transform carries out Analytical Pearson Residuals Normalization for UMI count matrix,
#' doi.org/10.1186/s13059-021-02451-7 .
#' @export
#' @param sce_object A SingleCellExperiment object.
#' @param theta A numerical value, default to 100. Set the measure of overdispersion to the Poisson distribution.
#' @return A SCE object with the normalized matrix added as alternative experiment under the name `Gene_Expression_PearNorm`.

do_AnPearson_transform <- function(sce_object, theta=100){
  counts_sum0 <- rowSums(assay(sce_object))
  counts_sum1 <- colSums(assay(sce_object))
  counts_sum <- sum(sce_object$sum)
  
  mu <- DelayedArray(crossprod(t(counts_sum0), counts_sum1) / counts_sum)
  z <- DelayedArray((assay(sce_object) - mu) / sqrt(mu + (mu**2/theta)))
  z <- replace(z, is.na(z), c(0))
  z <- z[, order(match(colnames(sce[, sce$qc=="passed"]), colnames(z)))]
  altExp(sce_object, "Gene_Expression_PearNorm") <- 
    SingleCellExperiment(list(count_AP=z), colData = colData(sce_object))
  sce_object
}

```



```{r eval=FALSE}
sce <- do_AnPearson_transform(sce[, sce$qc == "passed"])
```


```{r eval=FALSE}
sce <- swapAltExp(sce, "Gene_Expression_PearNorm")
```



```{r eval=FALSE}

sce <- runUMAP(sce, exprs_values="count_AP", 
                    name = "UMAP", BPPARAM=bp)
```



```{r eval=FALSE}
plotUMAP(sce, colour_by="Sox10", point_size=.05, by_exprs_values="count_AP") +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "grey", high = "blue") +
  coord_equal() +
  guides(colour=guide_legend(NULL, override.aes = list(size=2)))
```


![](umap_AnPearson.png)


# All-in-One

```{r}
source("src/lib_QC.R")
```

Another option is to call the holistic function `QC` which will handle everything for you. Just make sure to pass the appropriate parameters:

- sce_objec is a SingleCellExperiment object containing your count matrix as main experiment.

- organism, either "mouse" or "human", to target mitochondrial genes accordingly.

- hto, either `TRUE` or `FALSE` according to whether you have HTO tags on your experiment.

- methods, list of methods which can be passed to `GenerateCellHashingCalls()` to carry out demultiplexing.

- project, character string indicating the subfolder where to store graphical outputs. As default it is set to "New_folder", generating the path `pdf/1-Loading/New_project`.

- HTO_tag is a list containing the HTO tags one wants to keep.

- filter_singlet, either `TRUE` or `FALSE` to whether keep solely cell barcodes identified as singlet or not.

- mito_max, numeric value indicating the maximum cutoff for percentage of mitochondrial genes.

- min_nfeatures, numeric value indicating the minimum cutoff for number of features in log10 scale.

- normalization_method, method to choose as normalization strategy. The options are `logNorm`, `SCTransform` and `AnPearson`.




```{r warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
sce_2 <- QC(sce_object = sce,
            organism = "mouse",
            hto=TRUE,
            methods=c("multiseq","gmm_demux", "htodemux", "dropletutils"),
            project="test",
            HTO_tag=HTO_tag,
            filter_singlet=FALSE,
            mito_max=15,
            min_nfeatures=log10(200),
            normalization_method="logNorm",
            seed=12,
            workers = 16)
```
